CRIMES OF PASSION
This volume contains two short plays, The Ruffian on the Stair
and The Erpingham Camp, which were performed together as
a double bill at The Royal Court Theatre in June 1967. Joe
Orton died in August 1967 while this edition was in prep-
aration.
The staging of Crimes of Passion evoked from Ronald
Bryden in The Observer the comment that: ‘Orton has estab-
lised himself as a master-satirist of our national style of
gilding the verbal fig-leaf’. The surprising ‘crime of passion’
in The Ruffian on the Stair is arrived at after careful prep-
aration — emotional, circumstantial and practical — on the
part of the three characters. ‘The heart is situated just below
this badge on my pullover,’ the victim explains the day
before the crime. ‘Don’t miss will you?’ The Erpingham
Camp is a holiday camp where, as a result of an audience
participation event in doubtful taste, a rebellion breaks out
and a great man is martyred. His last words are: ‘I shall con-
fiscate your luggage. What is your chalet number ?’
Joe Orton’s characters grope their way through a series
of often painful situations in search of the appropriate turn
of phrase. The trouble they have with their vocabulary
reflects the trouble they have with their lives.

as Erpingham in the Rediffusion production of The Erpingham
